props.title: Get Out Your Handkerchiefs

sections.content: Bertrand Blier's provocative French comedy **Get Out Your Handkerchiefs** (1978) stunned audiences and critics by winning the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film. The film follows a bizarre love triangle that expands into a rectangle, pushing boundaries of sexual politics and social conventions. Like Blier's earlier **Going Places** (1974), it showcases his signature blend of outrageous humor and serious commentary on masculinity and relationships. The film stars Gérard Depardieu and Patrick Dewaere at their peak, continuing their electric screen partnership from **Going Places**.

sections.content: The film exemplifies the daring spirit of 1970s French cinema, alongside works like **The Mother and the Whore** (1973) and **La Grande Bouffe** (1973). These films challenged traditional morality while examining male insecurity and female autonomy. Blier's approach combines absurdist humor with genuine emotional depth, creating a unique tone that influenced later French filmmakers like Leos Carax and Gaspar Noé. The controversial subject matter - including a relationship with an underage boy - remains challenging even by today's standards.

The performances are extraordinary, particularly Carole Laure as the depressed wife Solange. Her deadpan delivery and mysterious demeanor create an enigmatic center around which the male characters orbit desperately. The film's examination of masculine possessiveness and competition recalls elements of François Truffaut's **Jules and Jim** (1962), though Blier's treatment is far more satirical and provocative. sections.content: Blier's film arrived at a crucial moment in French cinema, when the revolutionary spirit of May 1968 was giving way to more complex explorations of sexuality and gender roles. Like **La Cage aux Folles** (1978) from the same year, it challenged conventional morality while maintaining a comedic tone. The film's Oscar win represented a surprising mainstream acknowledgment of provocative European cinema, paving the way for other boundary-pushing foreign films to gain international recognition.
